heading: Spindle overheating
text:
CNC Milling Machine — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Spindle overheating
If the spindle temperature exceeds 70 °C during normal operation, stop the cycle and let the
spindle idle at low RPM to cool. The most common causes are insufficient spindle coolant flow, a
clogged coolant filter, worn spindle bearings, or running at high RPM for extended periods without
adequate warm-up. Check the coolant reservoir level and the filter first; a warm-up program of 10
minutes at gradually increasing RPM should be run at the start of every shift. Persistent overheating
after coolant checks usually points to bearing wear and should be escalated to a bearing inspection.

heading: Coolant system
text:
CNC Milling Machine — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Coolant system
The flood-coolant system requires the reservoir to be kept above the minimum line and the
concentration checked weekly with a refractometer (target 6–8% for general machining). Low
concentration causes rust and poor tool life; high concentration causes residue and foaming. Clean
the coolant filter weekly and replace it monthly. Symptoms of a coolant problem include poor surface
finish, smoking at the cut, rapid tool wear, and rust spots on the table.

heading: Way lubrication
text:
CNC Milling Machine — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Way lubrication
The linear ways and ballscrews are lubricated automatically by the central lube pump. Check the lube
reservoir daily and top up with the specified way oil (ISO VG 68). A low-lube alarm (see fault code
LUB-01) halts motion; do not bypass it. Symptoms of inadequate way lubrication include stick-slip
motion, position error, and audible squealing during rapid moves. Never substitute hydraulic oil for
way oil — it lacks the tackiness additives that keep the film on vertical ways.

heading: Tool changer faults
text:
CNC Milling Machine — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Tool changer faults
An automatic tool changer (ATC) that fails to complete a change usually reports fault code ATC-04
(arm timeout). Common causes are low air pressure (the ATC needs 6 bar minimum), a tool not seated
correctly in the pocket, or a mechanical obstruction. Verify shop air pressure at the machine
regulator, check that all pockets are clean and empty of chips, and confirm the tool holders are the
correct pull-stud type. Never reach into the ATC without applying lockout/tagout first.

heading: Axis position error / servo alarm
text:
CNC Milling Machine — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Axis position error / servo alarm
A position (following) error alarm means an axis could not keep up with its commanded position.
Causes range from mechanical (way lube failure, chip buildup, a crashed axis) to electrical (servo
drive fault, encoder problem). First check for obvious obstructions and confirm way lubrication.
Repeated following errors on one axis under light load suggest an encoder or drive issue and require
a service technician. Do not increase the following-error tolerance to silence the alarm.

heading: LUB-01 — Low lubrication
text:
Fault Code Reference — LUB-01 — Low lubrication
The central way-lube reservoir is below the minimum level or the lube pump has not built pressure.
Motion is halted for protection. Top up with the specified way oil (ISO VG 68) and confirm the pump
builds pressure; if it does not, check for a pump fault or a broken lube line. Do not bypass this
alarm — running the ways dry causes rapid, expensive wear.

heading: ATC-04 — Tool changer arm timeout
text:
Fault Code Reference — ATC-04 — Tool changer arm timeout
The automatic tool-changer arm did not complete its cycle in the allowed time. Usual causes: shop air
below 6 bar, a tool not seated in the pocket, chips in a pocket, or a mechanical obstruction. Apply
lockout/tagout before clearing any obstruction in the tool changer.

heading: TUR-02 — Turret index fault
text:
Fault Code Reference — TUR-02 — Turret index fault
The lathe turret failed to index or clamp. Check hydraulic pressure, clean chips from the coupling
teeth, and verify the clamp/unclamp solenoid. A turret that indexes but does not clamp firmly must
not be run in production, as it causes tool-position errors.

heading: HYD-07 — Low hydraulic pressure
text:
Fault Code Reference — HYD-07 — Low hydraulic pressure
Measured hydraulic pressure stayed below the commanded setpoint for more than three cycles. Check
fluid level and external leaks, verify the relief-valve setting with a calibrated gauge, and look for
internal leakage past a cylinder seal or a worn pump. Common on presses that have lost pressing
force.

heading: VIB-03 — Vibration alarm
text:
Fault Code Reference — VIB-03 — Vibration alarm
A machine's vibration exceeded its alarm level — either a hard breach of the fixed control limit or a
rolling z-score anomaly indicating early drift. Rule out imbalance, looseness, and misalignment
first; if the rising trend persists, schedule a bearing inspection at the next planned downtime.

heading: SPN-05 — Spindle overtemperature
text:
Fault Code Reference — SPN-05 — Spindle overtemperature
Spindle temperature exceeded its limit (typically 70 °C). Stop the cycle and idle to cool. Check
spindle coolant flow and the coolant filter; persistent overtemperature after coolant checks points
to bearing wear. Always run the shift-start warm-up program to avoid thermal shock.

heading: Loss of pressing force / pressure
text:
Hydraulic Press — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Loss of pressing force / pressure
A hydraulic press that will not build full tonnage usually has one of: low hydraulic fluid, a worn
pump, an internally leaking main cylinder seal, a relief valve set too low or stuck open, or air in
the system. Check the fluid level and look for external leaks first, then verify the relief-valve
setting against the machine spec with a calibrated gauge. A pressure that builds slowly and then
holds points to internal leakage past the cylinder seal; a pressure that will not build at all points
to the pump or relief valve. Fault code HYD-07 is logged when measured pressure stays below the
commanded setpoint for more than three cycles.

heading: Hydraulic fluid and filtration
text:
Hydraulic Press — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Hydraulic fluid and filtration
Use the specified anti-wear hydraulic oil (ISO VG 46) and keep it clean — over 70% of hydraulic
failures trace back to contaminated fluid. Check the fluid level daily, sample and test the fluid
quarterly, and change the return-line filter every 1000 operating hours or when the filter
differential-pressure indicator shows red. Cloudy or milky fluid indicates water contamination and
must be addressed before further operation. Keep the reservoir breather cap and its filter clean so
that dirt is not drawn in as the fluid level rises and falls.

heading: Overheating hydraulic oil
text:
Hydraulic Press — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Overheating hydraulic oil
Hydraulic oil above 60 °C degrades quickly and thins out, worsening internal leakage and force loss.
Causes of overheating include a low fluid level, a clogged cooler, a stuck-open relief valve
(dumping full flow across the valve as heat), or continuous operation above the duty rating. Check
the cooler and its coolant/air flow, confirm the fluid level, and verify the relief valve is not
weeping. Sustained high temperature accelerates seal aging and is a leading cause of the internal
leaks that later show up as lost tonnage.

heading: Slow or erratic ram motion
text:
Hydraulic Press — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Slow or erratic ram motion
Erratic, jerky, or slow ram movement is typically air in the hydraulic system or a failing pump.
Bleed the cylinder per the machine procedure, check the pump-suction line for leaks that could draw
air, and inspect the fluid for foaming. A ram that drifts down under load with the valve centered
indicates a leaking directional valve or cylinder seal and is also a safety concern — never work
under a ram held only by hydraulic pressure; use the mechanical safety blocks.

heading: Seal replacement
text:
Hydraulic Press — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Seal replacement
Main-cylinder seals are wear items. Signs that a seal needs replacement include external weeping at
the rod, a slow loss of holding pressure, and force that falls off over a production run as the oil
warms. Always relieve all stored pressure and apply lockout/tagout before opening a hydraulic
circuit, and cap open lines to keep contamination out during the repair.

heading: Chuck and workholding
text:
CNC Lathe — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Chuck and workholding
Hydraulic and pneumatic chucks must be greased through their grease fittings every 40 operating
hours; an ungreased chuck loses gripping force and can throw a part. Check the draw-bar pressure
against the machine spec before each production run. Symptoms of a workholding problem include parts
slipping in the cut, chatter marks, and inconsistent diameters. Never exceed the maximum chuck RPM
stamped on the chuck body — centrifugal force reduces grip as speed rises.

heading: Tailstock and centers
text:
CNC Lathe — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Tailstock and centers
The tailstock quill and the live center bearings should be checked for play monthly. A worn live
center bearing produces a squeal and a poor finish near the tailstock end of the part, and in the
worst case scores the center hole. Replace the live center at the first sign of runout above 0.01 mm.
Lubricate the quill with way oil and keep the taper bore clean and free of chips before mounting a
center.

heading: Spindle bearing wear
text:
CNC Lathe — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Spindle bearing wear
Spindle bearing wear on a lathe shows up as increased vibration, a rising spindle temperature, and a
degrading surface finish — often a periodic pattern in the finish that scales with spindle speed. A
rumbling or growling noise from the headstock at speed is a classic late-stage symptom. Confirm with
a vibration reading at the headstock (see the vibration guide): a steadily rising trend in the
overall velocity level is the reliable early indicator. Do not wait for the noise; replace bearings
on a condition-based schedule once the vibration trend crosses the alarm threshold.

heading: Turret indexing faults
text:
CNC Lathe — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Turret indexing faults
A turret that fails to index or locks between stations typically reports fault code TUR-02. Causes
include low hydraulic pressure, chips in the coupling teeth, or a clamp/unclamp solenoid fault. Clean
the turret face, verify hydraulic pressure, and cycle the turret manually in setup mode. A turret
that indexes but does not clamp firmly will produce tool-position errors and must not be run in
production.

heading: Poor surface finish
text:
CNC Lathe — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Poor surface finish
Poor surface finish on a lathe has several common causes: a worn or chipped insert, incorrect
feed/speed for the material, insufficient or misdirected coolant, excessive tool overhang, or
spindle bearing wear. Work through them cheapest-first: change the insert, verify the feed and
speed, and check coolant delivery before suspecting the spindle. A finish problem that is periodic
and speed-dependent, rather than random, points at the spindle bearings.

heading: Lockout / tagout (LOTO)
text:
Safety & Preventive Maintenance — Lockout / tagout (LOTO)
Before any maintenance that exposes you to hazardous energy — electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic,
stored spring or gravity — the machine must be locked out and tagged out. The sequence is: notify
affected operators, shut down the machine normally, isolate every energy source (main disconnect, air
supply, hydraulic pump), apply your personal lock and tag to each isolation point, release or block
stored energy (bleed hydraulic and pneumatic pressure, lower or block suspended members), and verify
zero energy by attempting a normal start. Each worker applies their own lock; never remove another
person's lock.

heading: Stored hydraulic and pneumatic energy
text:
Safety & Preventive Maintenance — Stored hydraulic and pneumatic energy
Hydraulic and pneumatic systems hold energy even after the machine is switched off. Before opening
any hydraulic or pneumatic circuit, relieve stored pressure through the bleed valves and confirm the
gauge reads zero. Never work under a hydraulic ram or press slide held only by pressure — insert the
mechanical safety blocks. Cap open hydraulic lines during a repair to keep contamination out.

heading: Daily checks
text:
Safety & Preventive Maintenance — Daily checks
At the start of every shift: check the way-lube reservoir, the coolant level and concentration, and
the hydraulic fluid level; run the spindle warm-up program; clear chips and swarf from the ways and
trays; and confirm guards and interlocks are in place and functioning. Log anything abnormal (noise,
leaks, alarms) rather than working around it.

heading: Preventive maintenance schedule
text:
Safety & Preventive Maintenance — Preventive maintenance schedule
A basic preventive-maintenance cadence: daily — levels, warm-up, chip clearing, guard checks; weekly
— coolant concentration and filter, clean swarf separators, check for leaks; monthly — grease chucks
and check tailstock/live-center play, replace coolant filters, inspect way covers; quarterly — sample
and test hydraulic and coolant fluids, check belt tension and alignment; and condition-based —
replace bearings when the vibration trend crosses its alarm level rather than on a fixed calendar.

heading: When to escalate
text:
Safety & Preventive Maintenance — When to escalate
Escalate to a service technician rather than continuing to run when: an axis reports repeated
following errors under light load (encoder/drive), a spindle overheats after coolant has been ruled
out (bearings), vibration keeps rising after imbalance and looseness are ruled out (bearings), or
hydraulic pressure cannot be restored after fluid, relief-valve, and leak checks (pump or internal
seal). Running through these to avoid downtime usually turns a planned repair into a larger unplanned
one.

heading: Wheel dressing and balance
text:
Surface Grinder — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Wheel dressing and balance
A grinding wheel must be dressed when the finish deteriorates, the wheel loads up (glazes), or
burning appears on the workpiece. Dress with a single-point diamond in light passes. A wheel that is
out of balance causes chatter and a wavy finish and accelerates spindle-bearing wear; balance the
wheel after mounting and after every dress if the machine has a balancing system. Always run a new
wheel at operating speed behind the guard for one minute before grinding (a ring test plus a spin
test), because a cracked wheel can burst.

heading: Burning and poor finish
text:
Surface Grinder — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Burning and poor finish
Burn marks (bluing) on the workpiece indicate too much heat at the wheel/work interface. Causes are a
glazed or loaded wheel, insufficient coolant, too heavy a down-feed, or too slow a traverse. Dress
the wheel, increase and aim the coolant at the grinding zone, and reduce the down-feed. A wavy or
chatter finish, as distinct from burning, points to wheel imbalance, spindle-bearing wear, or a loose
component rather than heat.

heading: Spindle vibration
text:
Surface Grinder — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Spindle vibration
Grinder spindles run at high speed and are sensitive to imbalance and bearing condition. Rising
vibration produces chatter marks and a poor finish long before any audible noise. Trend the spindle
vibration and act on the trend, not on a single reading — a steady climb in the overall velocity
level is the reliable early warning of bearing wear. Rebalance the wheel first (the cheap fix); if
vibration stays high with a balanced wheel, suspect the spindle bearings.

heading: Magnetic chuck
text:
Surface Grinder — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Magnetic chuck
The magnetic chuck holds the workpiece; weak holding lets parts shift and can throw them. Keep the
chuck face clean and free of nicks (stone it lightly if needed), and verify the demagnetize cycle
fully releases parts. A chuck that holds weakly may have a failing rectifier or coil; do not grind
with marginal holding force. Never rely on the magnet alone for tall or narrow parts — use back-up
blocks.

heading: Coolant and swarf
text:
Surface Grinder — Maintenance & Troubleshooting — Coolant and swarf
Grinding swarf is abrasive and must be kept out of the ways and the coolant. Clean the swarf tray and
magnetic separator daily, and keep the coolant clean and well-filtered — dirty coolant recirculates
abrasive that scores the work and wears the ways. Check that coolant reaches the grinding zone; a
blocked nozzle is a common cause of burning.

heading: Why trend vibration
text:
Vibration Monitoring & Bearing Wear (Condition-Based Maintenance) — Why trend vibration
Vibration is the earliest and most reliable indicator of rotating-machinery health. Bearing wear,
imbalance, misalignment, and looseness all raise vibration long before they produce audible noise or
a hard failure. The right practice is condition-based: trend the overall vibration velocity (mm/s
RMS) per machine over time and act when the trend rises, rather than waiting for a fixed threshold or
for the machine to fail. A steadily climbing trend is a stronger signal than any single reading.

heading: Bearing-wear signature
text:
Vibration Monitoring & Bearing Wear (Condition-Based Maintenance) — Bearing-wear signature
A degrading bearing produces a characteristic signature: the overall vibration level drifts upward
over days or weeks, with increasingly frequent short spikes, and the temperature of the housing
creeps up. This "slow climb with growing spikes" is the classic bearing-wear signature. On a machine
under condition monitoring, a rolling-window baseline (for example a 60-minute rolling mean and
standard deviation) lets you flag readings that deviate from a machine's own recent normal — catching
drift while the absolute value is still within the spec-sheet control limit, which a fixed threshold
would miss.

heading: Alarm thresholds vs. data-driven anomalies
text:
Vibration Monitoring & Bearing Wear (Condition-Based Maintenance) — Alarm thresholds vs. data-driven anomalies
Two complementary checks are used together. Fixed control limits (from the machine's spec sheet, e.g.
7 mm/s for a class of machine) alarm on any hard breach. A data-driven rolling z-score — how many
standard deviations a reading sits from the machine's own recent rolling mean — catches early drift
and spikes that are still inside the fixed limit. A reading flagged by the z-score but not yet past
the control limit is exactly the early warning that lets maintenance be scheduled before a breakdown.

heading: Responding to a rising trend
text:
Vibration Monitoring & Bearing Wear (Condition-Based Maintenance) — Responding to a rising trend
When a machine's vibration trend crosses its alarm level: first rule out the cheap causes —
imbalance (rebalance the wheel or tool), looseness (check mounting bolts), and misalignment. If the
trend persists with those ruled out, schedule a bearing inspection and replacement at the next
planned downtime rather than running to failure. Replacing a bearing on a planned stop costs a
fraction of the unplanned breakdown, the collateral damage, and the lost production of running it to
destruction.

heading: What to record
text:
Vibration Monitoring & Bearing Wear (Condition-Based Maintenance) — What to record
For each vibration alarm, record the machine ID, timestamp, the overall velocity level, the rolling
baseline at the time, and the action taken. This history is what turns reactive firefighting into a
predictive-maintenance program and lets you tune the alarm thresholds per machine class.
